It would appear that sqwṭ and its phonetic by-form ( when there is no intermediate vowel) zqwṭ are dissimilated forms of *zṭwṭ > sṭwṭ-- the latter a diminuitive from zwṭɁ which is a simplification of zwṭr which is a by-form or parallel development of the common Semitic root that appears most frequently in Aramaic as zʕr, "to be small."

notes.text: "Base" is the traditional interpretation of the Peshitta term at Gen. 6:16 and, hence, how it is used in subsequent literature. In its original context, however, it clearly is to be interpreted as following the Jewish interpretive tradition as an opening for light at the top of the ark. Hence, it is beyond any doubt a loanword from the quite common Akkadian architectural term samētu [pronounced something like /zwēd/ in Assyrian], "CAD (s.v. samītu): battlemented parapet," but probably better something like "ornamented protrusion of a wall".

citations.translation: he was an alert and careful guardian for his body

notes.text: In SamTgJ Gen 37:19, 24:65 זעיה renders Hebrew הלזה as a phonetic and midrashic play, taking it as if from the root ʕlz; see Tal under the peal finite form. The gloss "careful, wary" in LS2 is one of the very finest examples of the deranged semantic analysis often practiced by Brockelmann. The expression ܚܦܝܬܘܬܐ ܙܗܝܬܐ means "exceptional diligence"; there is nothing careful or wary about it other than what comes from the diligence of the head noun. This all-too-common practice in LS2 is very frustrating for the lexicographer and it is a shame that Sokoloff made few efforts to eliminate it.

notes.text: From the native lexicographers (see Audo p. 1:267)interpreted as a corrupt form from Greek ὑπόρριν, i.e. lit. "what is under the nose”, hence “mustache”. However since the only actual texts found so far with the word clearly suggest the meaning “tooth” of a key (or "ward" of the lock?), it is probable that the Arabic homograph سبلة has been misinterpreted as “mustache” instead of “spike”. Thus the word should be compared to the lexical variant suparinnu of the more common Akkadian supinnu “trowel” or the like, the same as Aramaic swpyn, i..e, “sharp point”. All of these forms belong to the non-Semitic stratum of cultural objects ending in -innu; see The Akkadian Influences on Aramaic, Assyriological Studies 19 (Chicago: Oriental Institute, 1974)')" onmouseout="toolTip()">AIOA
